title: Bacterial and Phage Genetics: Conjugation, Transduction and Transformation

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: An {{c1::auxotroph}} is a mutant that needs a nutrient added because it cannot make it; the wild type is a prototroph.
cards.quote: An auxotroph is a mutant that needs a nutrient added because it cannot make it; the wild type is a prototroph.

cards.front: Two E. coli K-12 strains, each an auxotroph for three different nutrients, are mixed and plated on minimal medium. A few colonies grow; neither strain alone gives any. Name two observations that make reversion a weaker explanation than recombination.
cards.back: Each parent lacked several abilities, so one lineage would need several reversions. Each parent plated alone gave no colonies, so reversion is not producing growth on its own.
cards.quote: A revertant mutates back to a working allele and can imitate a recombinant.

cards.front: In the Lederberg and Tatum cross, one strain needed threonine, leucine and thiamine and the other needed biotin, phenylalanine and cystine. Why does a colony on minimal medium show that genes came from both parents?
cards.back: The colony makes all six nutrients, but each parent lacked three. So it must carry working alleles from both parents: recombination between them.
cards.quote: A colony on bare minimal medium could make all six, so it carried working genes from both parents.

cards.front: In bacterial transformation, {{c1::competence}} is the physiological state that allows a recipient to take up free DNA.
cards.quote: Competence is a physiological state that allows uptake of free DNA.

cards.front: A cell-free filtrate from one bacterial strain transfers genes to another strain. Adding DNase to the filtrate abolishes the transfer. Which route of gene transfer fits, and in what state is the DNA?
cards.back: Transformation. The DNA is free in the medium and unprotected, so DNase destroys it. Cells are not needed, so the filtrate works. A phage coat would protect DNA from DNase.
cards.quote: Competence is a physiological state that allows uptake of free DNA.

cards.front: What two functions do the genes carried on the F plasmid of E. coli K-12 encode?
cards.back: A pilus and DNA transfer.
cards.quote: It carries genes for a pilus and for DNA transfer; other conjugative plasmids carry their own transfer genes.
cards.section: Conjugation: a chromosome enters in order

cards.front: F, the classic conjugation system of E. coli K-12, is a {{c1::plasmid}}, a small DNA circle that replicates separately from the chromosome.
cards.quote: F, the classic conjugation system of E. coli K-12, is a plasmid, a small DNA circle that replicates separately from the chromosome.
cards.section: Conjugation: a chromosome enters in order

cards.front: An F+ strain is mixed with an F- strain. Most F- cells become F+, yet very few gain chromosomal genes. Why?
cards.back: Transfer starts at the origin of transfer on F itself, so what moves is F. A free F rarely brings chromosome along.
cards.why: Chromosomal genes enter in quantity from an Hfr donor, where F sits in the chromosome.
cards.quote: In an F+ by F− cross, transfer starts from a fixed point on F, the origin of transfer.
cards.section: Conjugation: a chromosome enters in order

cards.front: In an Hfr by F- cross, why does the recipient rarely become Hfr or F+?
cards.back: The rest of F would enter last, and mating pairs usually break before the whole chromosome has crossed.
cards.quote: Because the rest of F would enter last and mating pairs usually break first, the recipient in an Hfr cross rarely becomes Hfr or F+.
cards.section: Conjugation: a chromosome enters in order

cards.front: In an interrupted-mating experiment, Wollman and Jacob broke Hfr by F- mating pairs apart at intervals. What was the recipient plated on, and what did streptomycin do?
cards.back: Recipients were plated on medium where only recombinants grew; streptomycin killed the donors, so only recipients that had received markers formed colonies at each time.
cards.quote: then plated the recipients on medium where only recombinants grew while streptomycin killed the donors
cards.section: Conjugation: a chromosome enters in order

cards.front: In an Hfr cross, why are markers that enter late recovered less often than markers that enter early?
cards.back: Mating pairs break as time passes, so fewer pairs are still connected when a late marker would cross.
cards.quote: Later markers are recovered less often as mating pairs break.

cards.front: An Hfr strain crossed with an F- recipient gives first appearance of j at 12 min, k at 19 min and m at 40 min. Assuming steady transfer, give the order and the gaps between neighbouring markers, then the distance from j to m.
cards.back: Order j-k-m. Gaps: 19-12 = 7 min and 40-19 = 21 min. Distance j to m: 40-12 = 28 min.
cards.why: Time gaps map distance when transfer is at a roughly steady rate.
cards.quote: Its order is a-b-c-d, with gaps of 6, 6 and 11 minutes.

cards.front: A second Hfr strain, mated with the same F- recipient at the same steady speed, gives d at 4 min, c at 15 min, b at 21 min and a at 27 min. The first strain gave a-b-c-d with gaps of 6, 6 and 11 min. What are this strain's gaps, and where does its transfer start?
cards.back: Order d-c-b-a with gaps of 11, 6 and 6 min: the same map read backwards. Its origin lies on the far side of d, about 4 min before d, and transfers in the opposite orientation.
cards.quote: Assume both transfer at the same steady speed, and that first appearance marks entry.

cards.front: How did Hfr strains with different marker orders show that the E. coli chromosome is a circle?
cards.back: Strains with different origins and orientations gave overlapping orders of markers. Fitted together, these orders closed into a circle.
cards.quote: Hfr strains with different origins and orientations produced overlapping orders that closed into a circle.

cards.front: What is the 0 to 100 minute scale of the E. coli map based on?
cards.back: It came from pooling many time-of-entry measurements. It is not a time that the chromosome always takes to cross.
cards.quote: a scale that came from pooling many time-of-entry measurements, not from a chromosome that always crosses in exactly the same time

cards.front: Two Hfr strains give the same marker order but transfer at consistently different speeds. Can their raw time gaps be overlaid as distances without recalibration?
cards.back: No. Time becomes distance only under the steady-transfer assumption. Different rates stretch the two time maps by different amounts, even when the order agrees.
cards.quote: Two Hfr strains give the same marker order but transfer at consistently different speeds.

cards.front: Two Hfr strains are mated with the same F- recipient at steady speed. Strain A gives x 7, y 15, z 26 min. Strain B gives z 3, y 14, x 22 min. Do they agree on the map, and where does B's origin lie?
cards.back: A: order x-y-z, gaps 8 and 11 min. B: order z-y-x, gaps 11 and 8 min. Same map read in opposite directions. B's origin lies about 3 min before z, on the side away from y.
cards.quote: its origin lies on the far side of d, about 4 minutes before d, and it transfers in the opposite orientation

cards.front: E. coli is haploid, so a recipient holding its own segment plus the matching donor segment is only briefly a {{c1::merozygote}}, or partial diploid.
cards.quote: E. coli is haploid, with one circular chromosome, so a recipient holding its own segment plus the matching donor segment is only briefly a merozygote, or partial diploid.

cards.front: In the simple linear-fragment model, why does stable replacement of a recipient segment in the circular chromosome need an even number of crossovers, at least two?
cards.back: A linear piece must be exchanged for the matching recipient segment, so a crossover is needed on each side of it.
cards.quote: stable replacement in the circular chromosome needs an even number of crossovers, at least two, one on each side

cards.front: After transduction, a donor piece that is not integrated may still be expressed briefly as an {{c1::abortive transductant}}, but it is not copied as cells divide.
cards.quote: After transduction, a piece that is not integrated may still be expressed briefly as an abortive transductant, but it is not copied as cells divide.

cards.front: An Hfr cross is repeated with a recipient that carries a recB mutation. Predict the number of recombinants recovered and explain.
cards.back: Fewer recombinants. Integration of donor DNA uses the recipient's recombination machinery, so a recipient defective in it integrates less, even though DNA still arrives.
cards.quote: recipients with a recB mutation yield fewer recombinants in Hfr crosses

cards.front: A temperate phage can kill its host or settle as a prophage; that settled state is called {{c1::lysogeny}}.
cards.quote: A temperate phage can kill its host or settle as a prophage, usually inserted into host DNA; that settled state is lysogeny.
cards.section: Transduction: host DNA inside a phage

cards.front: Zinder and Lederberg found genes passing between Salmonella typhimurium strains across a cell-blocking filter, and the agent resisted DNase. What did this show about the agent?
cards.back: It was not conjugation (no contact needed) and not free DNA (DNase did not stop it). It was a temperate phage carrying host DNA, later called P22.
cards.quote: found that genes passed between Salmonella typhimurium strains across a cell-blocking filter, and the agent resisted DNase
cards.section: Transduction: host DNA inside a phage

cards.front: P22 and P1 are {{c1::generalized}} transducers, which occasionally pack a random host-chromosome fragment in place of phage DNA.
cards.quote: P22 and P1 are generalized transducers, which occasionally pack a random host-chromosome fragment in place of phage DNA.
cards.section: Transduction: host DNA inside a phage

cards.front: Phage lambda transduces gal and bio genes of E. coli but almost never genes elsewhere on the chromosome. What explains this restriction?
cards.back: Lambda integrates at one attachment site between gal and bio. Inaccurate excision of the prophage can take adjacent host DNA, so only neighbours are carried: specialized transduction.
cards.quote: it integrates at a specific attachment site, between the gal and bio genes of E. coli K-12, and can take adjacent host DNA when the prophage excises inaccurately
cards.section: Transduction: host DNA inside a phage

cards.front: Among recipients selected for one donor marker, the fraction that also received another marker is the {{c1::cotransduction frequency}}.
cards.quote: the cotransduction frequency is the fraction of those selected for one donor marker that also received another

cards.front: Why can only genes that lie close together be cotransduced by P1?
cards.back: A P1 head holds about 100 kb, roughly 2 minutes of the 4.6-million-base-pair E. coli chromosome. Only genes within that span fit in one fragment.
cards.quote: A P1 head holds about 100 kb, roughly 2 minutes of the 4.6-million-base-pair E. coli chromosome, so only genes within that span can ride together.

cards.front: P1 grown on a wild-type donor infects an a b c triple mutant. Only a+ is selected. Of 400 a+ transductants, 240 are also b+ and 40 are also c+. Give both cotransduction frequencies. Which gene lies closer to a?
cards.back: b: 240/400 = 60%. c: 40/400 = 10%. Higher cotransduction means a shorter distance, so b lies closer to a.
cards.quote: Of 500 x+ transductants, 350 are also y+ and 100 are also z+.

cards.front: Cotransduction frequencies with one selected marker x are 70% for y and 20% for z. Why can these numbers not tell which side of x each gene lies on?
cards.back: They measure distance only. Both x-y-z and y-x-z fit, since closeness does not give direction. A three-factor class is needed to settle the order.
cards.quote: Two-factor data cannot say which side of x each marker occupies, so x-y-z and y-x-z both fit.

cards.front: Why is the relation between cotransduction frequency and distance not a straight line?
cards.back: Frequency also depends on fragment length and on recombination around each marker.
cards.quote: Cotransduction frequency also depends on fragment length and on recombination around each marker, so its relation to distance is nonlinear.

cards.front: P1 grown on a wild-type donor infects an a b c mutant, and a+ is selected. Classes among 300 transductants: a+ b+ c+ 150, a+ b c+ 90, a+ b+ c 10, a+ b c 50. Which gene order do these counts support, and why?
cards.back: Order a-c-b. The rarest class, a+ b+ c, would need four crossovers if c lies between a and b: it keeps a+ and b+ but not c. Check: c+ is 150+90 = 240 of 300 = 80%, b+ is 150+10 = 160 of 300, about 53%. The middle gene cotransduces more often than the outer one.
cards.quote: The middle gene, y, cotransduces more often than the outer gene z, as the order predicts.

cards.front: Two markers in E. coli lie about 40 minutes apart on the map. Would P1 cotransduction be a useful way to map the distance between them? What method would be?
cards.back: No. A P1 head carries about 2 minutes of chromosome, so markers 40 minutes apart never ride together. Interrupted mating, which orders genes around the whole chromosome by time of entry, would map them.
cards.quote: A P1 head holds about 100 kb, roughly 2 minutes of the 4.6-million-base-pair E. coli chromosome, so only genes within that span can ride together.

cards.front: Why does haploidy make bacteria convenient for finding recessive mutants?
cards.back: A haploid cell has no second allele to mask a recessive mutant genotype, so the phenotype shows. It may lag a few generations because a growing cell can carry several copies of its chromosome.
cards.quote: A haploid cell has no second allele to mask a recessive mutant genotype
cards.section: Why bacteria and phage made genetics fast

cards.front: How can a bacterial cross find one recombinant among many millions of cells?
cards.back: Selection does the searching: minimal medium or an antibiotic lets only cells with every selected ability grow.
cards.quote: Most important, selection does the searching: minimal medium or an antibiotic lets only cells with every selected ability grow, revealing one recombinant among many millions.
cards.section: Why bacteria and phage made genetics fast

cards.front: Phage are counted as {{c1::plaques}}, clear spots on a bacterial lawn, each beginning from one infectious unit under the assay conditions.
cards.quote: Each plaque, a clear spot on a bacterial lawn, begins from one infectious unit under the assay conditions, so phage are counted as plaques, and plaque appearance is a phenotype.
cards.section: Why bacteria and phage made genetics fast

cards.front: How can phage mutations be mapped by recombination, when phage have no mating?
cards.back: Two mutant phages infecting one cell can recombine, and the progeny are scored and mapped like progeny of a fly cross.
cards.quote: Two mutant phages infecting one cell can recombine, and their progeny map like a fly cross.
cards.section: Why bacteria and phage made genetics fast

cards.front: E. coli strains are separated in a U-shaped tube by a filter that stops cells while medium moves back and forth, and no recombinants appear. Adding DNase to a direct mixture of the strains does not reduce recombinants. What do the two results show together?
cards.back: Transfer needs cell contact, so it is conjugation. Transformation and transduction would cross the filter, and transformation would also be stopped by DNase.
cards.quote: separated E. coli strains in a U-shaped tube by a filter that stopped cells while medium moved back and forth; no recombinants appeared

cards.front: Prototrophs arise from a mixture of two auxotrophic strains. They still arise when cells are separated by a filter that passes DNA and phage, and DNase does not reduce them. Which route fits, and what protects the DNA?
cards.back: Transduction. The agent crosses a cell-blocking filter and resists DNase because a phage coat protects the DNA. Conjugation would be blocked by the filter and transformation would be stopped by DNase.
cards.quote: found that genes passed between Salmonella typhimurium strains across a cell-blocking filter, and the agent resisted DNase
cards.section: Transduction: host DNA inside a phage

cards.front: P1 grown on a wild-type donor transduces a recipient mutant at genes m and n. Among 1,000 m+ transductants, none is also n+. What does this suggest about m and n?
cards.back: They probably lie farther apart than one P1 fragment. Adjacent genes would show high cotransduction, and a finite sample only bounds the frequency.
cards.quote: A P1 head holds about 100 kb, roughly 2 minutes of the 4.6-million-base-pair E. coli chromosome, so only genes within that span can ride together.
